hints: Look closely at the reaction conditions, hot ethanolic NaOH is a classic clue that points to one type of mechanism over another.
Recall that aqueous NaOH favours substitution to form an alcohol, while ethanolic NaOH favours removal of HBr to form a double bond.
Remove H from a carbon next to the C-Br in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$ and join the carbons with a double bond to see which small alkene forms.
walkthrough:
**Spot the key conditions**

Great start, always read the conditions first. Hot ethanolic NaOH tells us $\text{OH}^-$ will act as a base, not as a nucleophile.

Condition rule: $$\text{ethanolic NaOH, heat} \rightarrow \text{elimination} \quad \text{vs} \quad \text{aqueous NaOH} \rightarrow \text{substitution}$$

**Apply elimination to 2-bromopropane**

In elimination, $\text{HBr}$ is removed from the haloalkane. We lose Br from C-2 and H from a neighbouring carbon, C-1 or C-3, to form a C=C double bond.

Reaction: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3 + \text{NaOH (ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Name the major product**

The three-carbon product with one double bond is propene. That is the elimination product, not an alcohol.

options.A: Propan-1-ol is incorrect. It is a primary alcohol that would require substitution with rearrangement, which does not happen here. Students sometimes pick any alcohol because they see NaOH and think of substitution.
options.B: Propan-2-ol is incorrect. This would be the substitution product if we used hot aqueous NaOH, where $\text{OH}^-$ replaces Br on C-2. The question uses ethanolic NaOH, so elimination wins instead.
options.C: 2-hydroxypropene is incorrect. This enol structure with both OH and C=C is not formed in this reaction and would be unstable. It is a distractor that mixes up substitution and elimination ideas.
options.D: Propene is correct. Hot ethanolic NaOH causes dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of 2-bromopropane, removing HBr to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$ as the major product.
